page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.se1.xlarge is a memory-optimized virtual machine instance configured with 4 vCPUs and 32 GB of RAM. Powered by an Intel Xeon 8269CY processor running at 2.5 GHz, the instance features 4 physical cores with a single thread per core on a dedicated CPU allocation. The x86_64 architecture supports AVX and AVX-512F vector extensions. This instance does not include local storage or GPU accelerators, relying entirely on network-attached storage and a baseline network bandwidth of 1 Gbps.

Benchmark data indicates that the ecs.se1.xlarge delivers modest processing and memory throughput. In stress-ng testing, both single-core and multi-core CPU performance fall into the bottom 25% of evaluated servers. Memory bandwidth benchmarks show similar limitations, with read-only large block transfers scoring in the bottom 10% and write operations in the bottom 25%. File compression and decompression tasks, such as single-threaded gzip and multi-threaded bzip3, also register in the lower percentiles, reflecting constraints in raw execution speed and memory bus efficiency.

The primary tradeoff of the ecs.se1.xlarge is its high memory-to-vCPU ratio of 8 GB per core, contrasted against its lower-tier computational performance. While it provides a generous memory footprint for applications requiring larger datasets in RAM, the underlying Intel Xeon 8269CY processor and memory subsystem operate with lower throughput compared to newer hardware generations. From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, this instance serves as a budget-friendly option for memory-intensive workloads that do not demand high CPU performance or rapid data processing speeds.

Given its hardware profile and benchmark results, the ecs.se1.xlarge is suited for memory-bound applications with low CPU utilization. Appropriate workloads include caching layers, lightweight in-memory databases like Redis with moderate transaction rates, and basic web serving. It is less suitable for CPU-intensive tasks, high-throughput database operations, or real-time data processing due to its lower performance in computational and memory bandwidth benchmarks.
